title: Rate limiting and backpressure
story:
A system with no way to refuse work accepts everything. Under excess demand it queues without bound, degrades for every caller equally, and eventually fails for all of them rather than for the portion it could not serve. Refusing deliberately is how you keep the failure proportional to the overload.

The protocol has a code for saying so. The 429 status indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, which the specification glosses as rate limiting. Response representations should include details explaining the condition, and may include a header indicating how long to wait before making a new request. That header is defined separately: servers send it to indicate how long the user agent ought to wait before a follow-up request, and its value can be either a date or a number of seconds.

Now the sentence that makes this lesson worth having, because it is the part that gets skipped. The specification is explicit that it does not define how the origin server identifies the user, nor how it counts requests. An origin server limiting request rates can do so based upon counts of requests on a per-resource basis, across the entire server, or even among a set of servers.

So the code is standardised and the policy is entirely yours, and every choice within it is a way of being unfair to somebody. Count per account and a single account behind a shared office address is throttled as one. Count per address and everyone behind that address shares a budget, including users who did nothing. Count per resource and a caller can saturate you by spreading across resources. Count across a set of servers and you need shared state on the hot path, which is a new dependency in the place you can least afford one; count per server and your effective limit is the stated one multiplied by the fleet size.

The distinction from backpressure is worth drawing because they are often used interchangeably. Rate limiting is a policy about who may send how much, applied at the edge and usually expressed per caller. Backpressure is a mechanism: a component that cannot keep up signals upstream to slow down, so the constraint propagates rather than being absorbed silently. A system with rate limits and no backpressure protects itself from callers and not from its own slow internals. A system with backpressure and no limits shares its capacity by whoever shouts loudest.

And the reason to reject rather than queue, which is the whole argument: a rejection with a stated retry time is information the caller can act on, while a request that waits indefinitely consumes resources on both sides and produces an answer nobody wants by the time it arrives.

problem.name: Load shedding
problem.shape: Demand arrives faster than the system can serve it, and accepting everything fails everybody rather than the excess.
tell: one caller can degrade the service for all others
queues grow without bound under peak load
there is no defined limit, only an implicit one discovered during incidents
a slow internal component has no way to signal upstream
problem.move: Set an explicit limit, reject above it with the code that says so, and tell the caller when to return. Choose the identity and the counting window deliberately, knowing each choice is unfair to a specific group. Add backpressure separately, so internal slowness propagates upstream instead of being absorbed by growing queues.
problem.invariant: The status code is standardised and the policy is not: the specification defines neither how the user is identified nor how requests are counted, so those are design decisions you own.
problem.breaks: Any counting scheme is unfair to somebody. Per-account penalises shared infrastructure, per-address penalises users who share it, per-resource lets a caller spread out to evade the limit, and counting across a fleet needs shared state on the hot path — which is a dependency exactly where you can least afford one.

cost.time: a counter check on every request, and shared-state coordination if the limit is fleet-wide
cost.space: per-identity counters with a window, which is memory proportional to the number of distinct callers
cost.beats: unbounded queueing, which converts a partial failure into a total one, and no limit at all, which lets one caller set everybody's experience

worked.problem: Why should a system under too much load reject work rather than queue it?
worked.reasoning:
Because a rejection is information the caller can act on, and a queued request is a resource commitment on both sides that usually produces a useless answer.

Take the queueing case first. Work arrives faster than it is served, so the backlog grows, and time-in-system grows with it — which is the previous lesson's arithmetic. Every item waiting occupies memory here and a pending connection, thread or timeout there. Eventually a request is served after the point at which its answer mattered: the user has left, the caller has timed out and retried, the result is stale. You spent the capacity anyway and delivered nothing. Worse, the degradation is spread evenly, so every caller gets an unusable experience rather than most callers getting a working one.

Rejecting inverts that. The portion of load you cannot serve is refused immediately, cheaply, and with a reason. The portion you can serve gets normal service. The failure is now proportional to the overload instead of total, which is the property you actually want under stress.

And the rejection carries information. The status code indicates the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, the representation should include details explaining the condition, and it may include a header saying how long to wait — a date or a number of seconds. A caller receiving that can back off intelligently, whereas a caller experiencing slowness cannot distinguish it from a network problem and will usually retry, adding load precisely when you have none to spare.

The part I would be careful to raise is that the standard defines the code and not the policy. It explicitly does not define how the origin server identifies the user, nor how it counts requests, and notes that limiting can be done per resource, across the whole server, or among a set of servers. So every real decision is yours, and each is unfair to someone: per account punishes shared infrastructure, per address punishes people who happen to share it, per resource lets a caller spread out to evade you, and fleet-wide counting needs shared state on the hot path — a new dependency where you can least afford one — while per-server counting means your real limit is the stated one times the fleet size.

I would also separate this from backpressure, since they get conflated. Rate limiting is a policy at the edge about who may send how much. Backpressure is a mechanism by which a component that cannot keep up signals upstream to slow down, so the constraint propagates rather than being silently absorbed. You need both: limits protect you from callers, backpressure protects you from your own slow internals.

problem.practice: Find out what happens when one caller sends ten times your expected rate — whether anything refuses it, and what other callers experience while it runs. Then write down which identity your limit counts against, and name the group that choice is unfair to.

beats.broke: Demand arrives faster than a system can serve it, and a system with no way to refuse work accepts everything, queues without bound, and fails for everybody rather than for the excess.
beats.fix: Refuse deliberately above a stated rate, telling the caller it was refused for that reason and when to return, so load that cannot be served is shed rather than absorbed.
beats.cost: The status code is standardised and the policy is not — who counts as a user, what is counted, and over what window are all yours to define, and every choice is a way of being unfair to somebody.

interview.q: Why should a system under too much load reject work rather than queue it?
interview.trap: Framing it as protecting the server. The stronger argument is about the caller: a rejection with a retry time is actionable information, while slowness is indistinguishable from a network fault and provokes retries that add load exactly when there is none to spare.
